/-!
# The low-degree game

This file introduces the finite question and answer alphabets used by the
low-degree component of the Pauli basis test.  The maps are explicit maps on
the ambient coefficient space; their conditional-linearity and distribution
invariants are recorded as proof-level obligations for later stages.

## References

The source-facing nodes are `def:ld-game`, `def:ld-question-distribution`, and
`def:ld-win-predicate` in
`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:17-105`; their paper origin is
`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:958-1010`.
-/

open scoped BigOperators

namespace MIPStarRE.QPBT

open MIPStarRE.LDT

/-- Parameters for the low-degree game, including the fixed field model used by
the ambient coefficient space.  This is the Lean carrier for `def:ld-game` in
`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:17-105`, with paper origin
`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:958-1010`.
-/
structure LdParams where
  q : ℕ
  m : ℕ
  d : ℕ
  k : ℕ
  hm : 1 ≤ m
  hd : 1 ≤ d
  hk : 1 ≤ k
  hq : IsAdmissibleSize q
  hdvd : m ∣ q
  model : FixedFieldModel q

/-- The scalar carrier selected by an `LdParams` record; this is the fixed
field carrier in `def:ld-game`, blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:17-31`, paper
origin `references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:958-961`.
-/
abbrev ScalarQ (P : LdParams) := P.model.K

/-- The three low-degree question types of `def:ld-game`, blueprint
`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:17-31`, paper origin
`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:958-961`.
-/
inductive LdType where
  | point
  | aline
  | dline
  deriving DecidableEq, Repr, Inhabited, Fintype

/-- The register index used by the low-degree game (`def:ld-game`, blueprint
`ch13_qpbt_test.tex:17-31`; paper origin
`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:958-961`).
-/
abbrev LdIndex (P : LdParams) := (Fin P.m ⊕ Unit) ⊕ Fin P.m

/-- The full ambient low-degree coefficient space (`def:ld-game`, blueprint
`ch13_qpbt_test.tex:17-31`; paper origin
`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:958-961`).
-/
abbrev LdSpace (P : LdParams) := LdIndex P → ScalarQ P

/-- The point coordinates of an ambient low-degree vector in
`def:ld-question-distribution`, blueprint
`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:38-49`, paper origin
`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:979-1009`.
-/
def LdSpace.point (z : LdSpace P) : Fin P.m → ScalarQ P :=
  fun i => z (.inl (.inl i))

/-- The shared scalar coordinate of an ambient low-degree vector in
`def:ld-question-distribution`, blueprint
`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:38-49`, paper origin
`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:979-1009`.
-/
def LdSpace.seed (z : LdSpace P) : ScalarQ P :=
  z (.inl (.inr ()) )

/-- The direction coordinates of an ambient low-degree vector in
`def:ld-question-distribution`, blueprint
`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:38-49`, paper origin
`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:979-1009`.
-/
def LdSpace.direction (z : LdSpace P) : Fin P.m → ScalarQ P :=
  fun i => z (.inr i)

/-- The integer-coordinate map `χ` from the fixed field representation.  This
is `eq:chi-func` in `def:ld-question-distribution`, blueprint
`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:38-49`, paper origin
`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:979-1009`.
-/
noncomputable def chiIndex (P : LdParams) (s : ScalarQ P) : Fin P.m := by
  letI : NeZero P.m := ⟨by
    exact Nat.ne_of_gt (lt_of_lt_of_le Nat.zero_lt_one P.hm)⟩
  exact Fin.ofNat P.m ((binaryRepresentation P.model s).val / (P.q / P.m))

/-- The source uses the block quotient of the fixed integer representation.  The
`Fin.ofNat` wrapper supplies the totalized boundary behavior for the temporary
 skeleton's proof-irrelevant zero-dimension branch.  This is the projection
 clause of `def:ld-question-distribution`, blueprint
 `blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:38-49`, paper origin
 `references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:979-1009`.
-/
def prefixProjection (i : Fin P.m) (v : Fin P.m → ScalarQ P) :
    Fin P.m → ScalarQ P :=
  fun j => if j.val < i.val then 0 else v j

/-- The point CL map, retaining the point block and clearing the auxiliary
blocks.  It is the map `L_point` of `def:ld-question-distribution`, blueprint
`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:38-49`, paper origin
`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:979-1009`.
-/
def ldPointCL (P : LdParams) (z : LdSpace P) : LdSpace P :=
  fun i => match i with
  | .inl (.inl j) => z (.inl (.inl j))
  | .inl (.inr _) => 0
  | .inr _ => 0

/-- The affine-line CL map.  The direction block is put through the canonical
line representative map from `def:line-representative`, while the point block
is retained (blueprint `blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:38-49`; paper
origin `references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:979-1009`).
-/
noncomputable def ldALineCL (P : LdParams) (z : LdSpace P) : LdSpace P :=
  let i := chiIndex P (z.seed)
  let rep := lineRepMap (coordinateDirection i)
  fun i => match i with
  | .inl (.inl j) => (rep (z.point)) j
  | .inl (.inr _) => z (.inl (.inr ()))
  | .inr _ => 0

/-- The diagonal-line CL map, using the same canonical representative interface
for the direction block.  This is the `L_DLine` clause of
`def:ld-question-distribution` (blueprint
`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:38-49`; paper origin
`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:979-1009`).
-/
noncomputable def ldDLineCL (P : LdParams) (z : LdSpace P) : LdSpace P :=
  let i := chiIndex P (z.seed)
  let direction := prefixProjection i (z.direction)
  let rep := lineRepMap direction
  fun i => match i with
  | .inl (.inl j) => (rep (z.point)) j
  | .inl (.inr _) => z (.inl (.inr ()))
  | .inr j => direction j

/-- Dispatch the three low-degree CL maps by question type.  This is the typed
construction in `def:ld-question-distribution`, blueprint
`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:38-49`, paper origin
`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:979-1009`.
-/
noncomputable def ldCL (P : LdParams) : LdType → LdSpace P → LdSpace P
  | .point => ldPointCL P
  | .aline => ldALineCL P
  | .dline => ldDLineCL P

/-- The conditional-linearity level of the affine-line map.  This is a named
Lean proof obligation for the prose assertion in `def:ld-question-distribution`,
blueprint `blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:38-49`, paper
`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:979-1009`.
-/
theorem isCondLinear_ldALineCL (P : LdParams) :
    IsCondLinearOn (ScalarQ P) Finset.univ 2 (ldALineCL P) := by
  sorry

/-- The conditional-linearity level of the diagonal-line map.  This is the
level-3 assertion in `def:ld-question-distribution`, blueprint
`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:38-49`, paper origin
`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:979-1009`.

/-!
# The Magic Square game

The Magic Square component is represented by finite constraint and variable
question types, the incidence graph, and the two corresponding answer forms.
Its rigidity theorem is outside the stage-4.1 statement closure; only the game
carrier is needed here.

## References

This file formalizes `def:ms-game` in
`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:188-203`, from
`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:512-610`.
-/

namespace MIPStarRE.QPBT

open MIPStarRE.LDT

/-- A Magic Square question is either a row/column constraint or a cell
variable.  This is `def:ms-game`, blueprint lines 188-203, paper origin
`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:1050-1069`.
-/
inductive MsType where
  | constraint (i : Fin 6)
  | var (j : Fin 9)
  deriving DecidableEq, Repr, Inhabited, Fintype

/-- The cell incident to a constraint and one of its three positions in
`def:ms-game`, blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:188-203`, paper origin
`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:1050-1069`.
-/
def msConstraintVars (i : Fin 6) (j : Fin 3) : Fin 9 :=
  ⟨if i.val < 3 then i.val * 3 + j.val else i.val - 3 + j.val * 3, by
    by_cases h : i.val < 3 <;> simp [h] <;> omega⟩

/-- The exceptional Magic Square parity, equal to one only on the final
constraint.  Blueprint `blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:188-203`; paper
origin `references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:1050-1069`.
-/
def msParity (i : Fin 6) : ZMod 2 :=
  if i.val = 5 then 1 else 0

/-- The 18 constraint-variable incidence edges of the Magic Square graph in
`def:ms-game`, blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:188-203`, paper origin
`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:1050-1069`.
-/
def msEdges : Finset (Sym2 MsType) :=
  (Finset.univ : Finset (Fin 6 × Fin 3)).image (fun ij =>
    Sym2.mk (.constraint ij.1) (.var (msConstraintVars ij.1 ij.2)))

/-- A Magic Square answer is a parity triple or a single cell bit, as prescribed
by `def:ms-game`, blueprint `blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:188-203`,
paper origin `references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:1050-1069`.
-/
inductive MsAnswer where
  | triple (β : Fin 3 → ZMod 2)
  | bit (γ : ZMod 2)
  deriving DecidableEq

/-- A finite code for the two Magic Square answer constructors.  This is
Lean-only carrier infrastructure for `def:ms-game`, blueprint
`ch13_qpbt_test.tex:188-203`, paper origin
`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:1050-1069`.
-/
abbrev MsAnswerCode := (Fin 3 → ZMod 2) ⊕ ZMod 2

/-- The constructor-preserving code equivalence for `MsAnswer`; Lean-only
finite-carrier infrastructure for `def:ms-game`, blueprint
`ch13_qpbt_test.tex:188-203`, paper origin
`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:1050-1069`.
-/
noncomputable def msAnswerEquiv : MsAnswer ≃ MsAnswerCode where
  toFun
    | .triple β => .inl β
    | .bit γ => .inr γ
  invFun
    | .inl β => .triple β
    | .inr γ => .bit γ
  left_inv := by intro x; cases x <;> rfl
  right_inv := by
    intro x
    cases x <;> rfl

noncomputable instance : Fintype MsAnswer :=
  Fintype.ofEquiv MsAnswerCode msAnswerEquiv.symm

instance : Inhabited MsAnswer := ⟨.bit 0⟩

/-- The Magic Square consistency predicate.  Constructor mismatches are
rejected, as required by `def:ms-game` (blueprint lines 188-203; paper
`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:1050-1069`).
-/
def msWinPredicate :
    MsType → MsType → MsAnswer → MsAnswer → Bool
  | .constraint i, .constraint j, .triple β, .triple β' =>
      decide (i = j ∧ β = β')
  | .var i, .var j, .bit γ, .bit γ' =>
      decide (i = j ∧ γ = γ')
  | .constraint i, .var j, .triple β, .bit γ =>
      decide
        ((∑ k : Fin 3, β k) = msParity i ∧
          ∃ k : Fin 3, msConstraintVars i k = j ∧ β k = γ)
  | .var j, .constraint i, .bit γ, .triple β =>
      decide
        ((∑ k : Fin 3, β k) = msParity i ∧
          ∃ k : Fin 3, msConstraintVars i k = j ∧ β k = γ)
  | _, _, _, _ => false

/-- The Magic Square game as a finite `Game`.  This is `def:ms-game` in
`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:188-203`, paper origin
`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:1050-1069`.
-/
noncomputable def msGame : Game where
  QuestionA := MsType
  QuestionB := MsType
  AnswerA := MsAnswer
  AnswerB := MsAnswer
  μ := graphDistribution msEdges (by sorry)
  μ_prob := by sorry
  decide := msWinPredicate

end MIPStarRE.QPBT
`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:1012-1039`.
-/
def pauliPointPairCondition (P : AdmissibleParams) (W : PauliKind)
    (z : PauliSpace P) (a : PauliScalar P) (β : ZMod 2) : Prop :=
  pauliPairGamma P z ≠ 0 ∨
    fixedBinTrace P.model
      (a * (match W with
      | .X => pauliRXBlock z
      | .Z => pauliRZBlock z)) = β

/-- The Point/Variable consistency clause of `def:pauli-win-predicate`.
The check is gated by `gamma = 0` and only uses Variable 1 in the X basis or
Variable 5 in the Z basis.  Blueprint
`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:331-367`; paper origin
`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:1012-1039`.
-/
def pauliPointVariableCondition (P : AdmissibleParams) (W : PauliKind)
    (z : PauliSpace P) (j : Fin 9) (a : PauliScalar P) (β : ZMod 2) : Prop :=
  pauliPairGamma P z = 0 ∨
    (j = ⟨0, by decide⟩ ∧ W = .X ∧
        fixedBinTrace P.model (a * pauliRXBlock z) = β) ∨
    (j = ⟨4, by decide⟩ ∧ W = .Z ∧
        fixedBinTrace P.model (a * pauliRZBlock z) = β)

/-- The Pauli win predicate, with constructor-shape rejection.  This is
`def:pauli-win-predicate` in `blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:331-367`,
paper origin `references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:1012-1039`.
-/
noncomputable def pauliWinPredicate (P : AdmissibleParams) :
    PauliQuestion P → PauliQuestion P → PauliAnswer P → PauliAnswer P → Bool :=
  open Classical in
  fun (tA, xA) (tB, xB) a b =>
    if validPauliAnswer tA a && validPauliAnswer tB b then
      match tA, tB, a, b with
      | .point W, .point W', .value u, .value v =>
          decide (W = W' ∧ u = v)
      | .aline W, .point W', .alinePoly f, .value u =>
          decide (W = W' ∧ pauliAlinePointCondition P W xA xB f u)
      | .point W, .aline W', .value u, .alinePoly f =>
          decide (W = W' ∧ pauliAlinePointCondition P W xB xA f u)
      | .dline W, .point W', .dlinePoly f, .value u =>
          decide (W = W' ∧ pauliDlinePointCondition P W xA xB f u)
      | .point W, .dline W', .value u, .dlinePoly f =>
          decide (W = W' ∧ pauliDlinePointCondition P W xB xA f u)
      | .point W, .pauli W', .value u, .pauliOutcome h =>
          decide (W = W' ∧ pauliPointPauliCondition P W xA h u)
      | .pauli W, .point W', .pauliOutcome h, .value u =>
          decide (W = W' ∧ pauliPointPauliCondition P W xB h u)
      | .pairW W, .pair, .bit β, .pairBits bits =>
          decide (pauliPairCondition P W xA β bits)
      | .pair, .pairW W, .pairBits bits, .bit β =>
          decide (pauliPairCondition P W xB β bits)
      | .point W, .pairW W', .value u, .bit β =>
          decide (W = W' ∧ pauliPointPairCondition P W xB u β)
      | .pairW W, .point W', .bit β, .value u =>
          decide (W = W' ∧ pauliPointPairCondition P W xA u β)
      | .ms t, .ms t', .msTriple u, .msTriple v =>
          decide (t = t' ∧ u = v)
      | .ms t, .ms t', .bit u, .bit v =>
          decide (t = t' ∧ u = v)
      | .ms (.constraint i), .ms (.var j), .msTriple β, .bit γ =>
          decide (pauliPairGamma P xA = 0 ∨
            msWinPredicate (.constraint i) (.var j) (.triple β) (.bit γ))
      | .ms (.var j), .ms (.constraint i), .bit γ, .msTriple β =>
          decide (pauliPairGamma P xB = 0 ∨
            msWinPredicate (.var j) (.constraint i) (.bit γ) (.triple β))
      | .point W, .ms (.var j), .value u, .bit β =>
          decide (pauliPointVariableCondition P W xB j u β)
      | .ms (.var j), .point W, .bit β, .value u =>
          decide (pauliPointVariableCondition P W xA j u β)
      | .aline W, .aline W', .alinePoly f, .alinePoly g => decide (W = W' ∧ f = g)
      | .dline W, .dline W', .dlinePoly f, .dlinePoly g => decide (W = W' ∧ f = g)
      | .pauli W, .pauli W', .pauliOutcome u, .pauliOutcome v =>
          decide (W = W' ∧ u = v)
      | .pairW W, .pairW W', .bit u, .bit v => decide (W = W' ∧ u = v)
      | .pair, .pair, .pairBits u, .pairBits v => decide (u = v)
      | _, _, _, _ => true
    else false

/-- The Pauli basis test game.  This is `def:pauli-question-distribution` and
`def:pauli-win-predicate` packaged as the symmetric game of
`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:285-367`, paper origin
`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:979-1039`.
-/
noncomputable def pauliBasisTest (P : AdmissibleParams) : Game where
  QuestionA := PauliQuestion P
  QuestionB := PauliQuestion P
  AnswerA := PauliAnswer P
  AnswerB := PauliAnswer P
  μ := pauliQuestionDistribution P
  μ_prob := by sorry

# Games, tensor-product strategies, and value

This file provides the finite game carrier used by the Pauli basis test.  Pure
states are vectors in `EuclideanSpace`, and POVMs use the project's matrix
`Measurement` structure.

## References

The source-facing nodes are `def:game`, `def:povm-conventions`,
`def:tensor-product-strategy`, and `def:tensor-product-value` in
`blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:47-82` and `8-26`.
The paper origin is `references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:219-271`.
-/

open scoped BigOperators Matrix ComplexOrder

namespace MIPStarRE.QPBT

open MIPStarRE.LDT
open MIPStarRE.Quantum

/--
A finite two-player one-round game with a probability distribution on question
pairs and a Boolean decision predicate.  This is `def:game` in
`blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:51-59`, with paper origin
`references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:1-80`.
-/
structure Game where
  QuestionA : Type
  QuestionB : Type
  AnswerA : Type
  AnswerB : Type
  [questionAFintype : Fintype QuestionA]
  [questionBFintype : Fintype QuestionB]
  [answerAFintype : Fintype AnswerA]
  [answerBFintype : Fintype AnswerB]
  [questionADecidableEq : DecidableEq QuestionA]
  [questionBDecidableEq : DecidableEq QuestionB]
  [answerADecidableEq : DecidableEq AnswerA]
  [answerBDecidableEq : DecidableEq AnswerB]
  μ : Distribution (QuestionA × QuestionB)
  μ_prob : μ.IsProbability
  decide : QuestionA → QuestionB → AnswerA → AnswerB → Bool

attribute [instance] Game.questionAFintype Game.questionBFintype
  Game.answerAFintype Game.answerBFintype Game.questionADecidableEq
  Game.questionBDecidableEq Game.answerADecidableEq Game.answerBDecidableEq

/--
The marginal of a joint POVM obtained by post-processing its answer pair.  This
is the POVM convention of `def:povm-conventions` in
`blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:8-26`; the post-processing operation
is the already formalized `Measurement.postprocess`, with paper origin
`references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:1-80`.
-/
noncomputable def marginalLeft {α β d : Type*}
    [Fintype α] [Fintype β] [DecidableEq α] [DecidableEq β]
    [Fintype d] [DecidableEq d]
    (M : Measurement (α × β) d) : Measurement α d :=
  M.postprocess Prod.fst

/-- The right marginal of a joint POVM, obtained using `Prod.snd` in
`def:povm-conventions`, `blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:8-26`,
paper origin `references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:1-80`.
-/
noncomputable def marginalRight {α β d : Type*}
    [Fintype α] [Fintype β] [DecidableEq α] [DecidableEq β]
    [Fintype d] [DecidableEq d]
    (M : Measurement (α × β) d) : Measurement β d :=
  M.postprocess Prod.snd

/-- Projectivity of every effect in a POVM (`def:povm-conventions`, blueprint
`blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:8-26`; paper origin
`references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:1-80`). -/
def Measurement.IsProjective {α d : Type*} [Fintype α] [Fintype d] [DecidableEq d]
    (M : Measurement α d) : Prop :=
  ∀ a, IsProj (M.effect a)

/--
The tensor-product strategy of `def:tensor-product-strategy` in
`blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:61-69` (paper origin
`references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:1-80`).
-/
structure Strategy (G : Game) where
  ιA : Type
  ιB : Type
  [ιAFintype : Fintype ιA]
  [ιBFintype : Fintype ιB]
  [ιADecidableEq : DecidableEq ιA]
  [ιBDecidableEq : DecidableEq ιB]
  ψ : EuclideanSpace ℂ (ιA × ιB)
  ψ_norm : ‖ψ‖ = 1
  A : G.QuestionA → Measurement G.AnswerA ιA
  B : G.QuestionB → Measurement G.AnswerB ιB

attribute [instance] Strategy.ιAFintype Strategy.ιBFintype
  Strategy.ιADecidableEq Strategy.ιBDecidableEq

/-- The rectangular tensor placement used in strategy probabilities.  This is
the finite-matrix realization of `def:tensor-product-strategy`, blueprint
`blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:61-69`; paper origin
`references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:1-80`.
-/
def heteroKron {ιA ιB : Type*} (A : Op ιA) (B : Op ιB) : Op (ιA × ιB) :=
  Matrix.kronecker A B

/- The Euclidean linear map is the shared action used by the value and distance
functionals.  Keeping it at the Euclidean-space level avoids accidentally
using the function-space supremum norm of `Matrix.mulVec`. -/
/-- Apply a finite matrix to a Euclidean-space state.  This is the Hilbert-space
action underlying `def:tensor-product-value`, paper
`references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:219-271`. -/
noncomputable def applyOperatorToState {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι]
    (M : Op ι) (ψ : EuclideanSpace ℂ ι) : EuclideanSpace ℂ ι :=
  Matrix.toEuclideanLin M ψ

/-- The Born weight of an answer pair for a strategy.  Lean-only support for
`def:tensor-product-value`, blueprint `ch12_qpbt_games.tex:71-82`, paper
`references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:219-271`. -/
private noncomputable def outcomeWeight {G : Game} (S : Strategy G)
    (x : G.QuestionA) (y : G.QuestionB) (a : G.AnswerA) (b : G.AnswerB) : ℝ :=
  let M : MIPStarRE.Quantum.Op (S.ιA × S.ιB) :=
    heteroKron ((S.A x).effect a) ((S.B y).effect b)
  let acted := applyOperatorToState M S.ψ
  (inner ℂ S.ψ acted).re

/--
The tensor-product value, expressed as the distribution average of the Born
probabilities.  This is `def:tensor-product-value` in
`blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:71-82`, with paper origin
`references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:1-80`.
-/
noncomputable def Strategy.value {G : Game} (S : Strategy G) : ℝ :=
  avgOver G.μ (fun xy =>
    ∑ a : G.AnswerA, ∑ b : G.AnswerB,
      if G.decide xy.1 xy.2 a b then outcomeWeight S xy.1 xy.2 a b else 0)

/--
The tensor-product game value as a conditional supremum over all finite
strategies.  The `sSup (Set.range ...)` form is the csSup formulation requested
for `def:tensor-product-value`, blueprint
`blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:71-82`, paper origin
`references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:1-80`; attainment is
intentionally not asserted here.
-/
noncomputable def Game.value (G : Game) : ℝ :=
  sSup (Set.range (fun S : Strategy G => S.value))

end MIPStarRE.QPBT

estimates to later proof stages.

## References

-/

open scoped BigOperators

namespace MIPStarRE.QPBT

open MIPStarRE.LDT
open MIPStarRE.Quantum

/--
Squared Euclidean distance between pure states.  Blueprint `def:state-distance`
(`blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:171-179`), paper origin
`references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:95-103`.
-/
noncomputable def stateDistSq {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι]
    [DecidableEq ι]
    (ψ φ : EuclideanSpace ℂ ι) : ℝ :=
  ‖ψ - φ‖ ^ 2

/--
Average squared state-dependent distance between two operator families.  This
is `def:povm-distance` in `blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:203-210`,
with paper origin `references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:95-103`.
-/
noncomputable def opFamilyDistSq {X α ι : Type*}
    [Fintype α] [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
    (μ : Distribution X) (M N : X → α → Op ι)
    (ψ : EuclideanSpace ℂ ι) : ℝ :=
  avgOver μ (fun x =>
    ∑ a : α, ‖applyOperatorToState (M x a - N x a) ψ‖ ^ 2)

end MIPStarRE.QPBT

   653	\subsubsection{Bit string representations}
   654	\label{sec:ff-representations}
   655	
   656	As mentioned at the end of \Cref{sec:tms}, we sometimes treat the
   657	inputs and outputs of Turing machines as representing elements of a finite
   658	field, or a vector space over a finite field.
   659	We discuss some important details about bit representations of finite field
   660	elements and arithmetic over finite fields.
   661	
   662	In the paper we only consider fields $\F_{2^k}$ where $k$ is odd. 
   663	
   664	\begin{definition}\label{def:admissible-size}
   665	  A field size $q$ is called an \emph{admissible} field size if $q=2^k$ for odd
   666	  $k$.
   667	\end{definition}
   668	
   669	Elements of $\F_2$ are naturally represented using bits. 
   670	To represent elements of $\F_{2^k}$ as binary strings we require the
   671	specification of a basis of $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$.
   672	Given a basis $\{e_i\}_{i=1}^k$ of $\F_{2^k}$, every element $a \in \F_{2^k}$
   673	has a unique expansion $a = \sum_{i=1}^k a_i e_i$ and can be represented as the
   674	$k$-bit string corresponding to $\downsize(a) \in \F_2^k$.
   675	Note that we omitted the subscript $2$ of $\downsize$ as it maps to the linear
   676	space over the prime subfield $\F_2$.
   677	Thus the \emph{binary representation} of $a \in \F_{2^k}$ is defined as the
   678	natural binary representation of $\downsize(a) \in \F_2^k$ (which in turn is the
   679	\emph{$\F_2$-representation of $a$}).
   680	Throughout the paper we freely associate between the binary representation of a
   681	field element $a \in \F_{2^k}$ and its $\F_2$-representation,
   682	although---technically speaking---these are distinct objects.
   683	
   684	Given the representations $\downsize(a), \downsize(b)$ of $a, b \in \F_{2^k}$, to
   685	compute the binary representation of $a+b$ it suffices to compute the addition
   686	bit-wise, modulo $2$.
   687	Computing the multiplication of elements $a, b$ requires the specification of
   688	the multiplication tables $\{K_{e_i} \in \Matrix_k (\F_2)\}_{i=1}^k $ for the
   689	basis $\{e_i\}$.
   690	Given representations $\downsize(a) = (a_i)_{i=1}^k$, $\downsize(b) =
   691	(b_i)_{i=1}^k$ for $a, b \in \F_{2^k}$ respectively, the representation
   692	$\downsize(ab)$ of the product $ab$ is computed as
   693	\begin{equation}
   694	  \label{eq:eq-mult}
   695	  \downsize(ab) = \sum_{i=1}^k \, a_i \, \downsize \bigl( e_i b \bigr) =
   696	  \sum_{i=1}^k \, a_i \bigl( K_{e_i}\, \downsize (b) \bigr)\;.
   697	\end{equation}
   698	Thus, using our representation for field elements, efficiently performing finite
   699	field arithmetic in $\F_{2^k}$ reduces to having access to the multiplication
   700	table of some basis of $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$.
   701	
   702	The following fact provides an efficient deterministic algorithm for computing a
   703	self-dual normal basis for $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$ and the corresponding
   704	multiplication tables for any odd $k$.
   705	
   706	\begin{lemma}
   707	  \label{lem:efficient_basis}
   708	  There exists a deterministic algorithm that given an odd integer $k > 0$,
   709	  outputs a self-dual normal basis of $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$ and the
   710	  multiplication tables of the basis in $\poly(k)$ time.
   711	\end{lemma}
   712	
   713	\begin{proof}
   714		The algorithm of Shoup~\cite[Theorem 3.2]{shoup1990new} shows that for prime
   715	  $p$, an irreducible polynomial in $\Fp[X]$ of degree $k$ can be computed in
   716	  time $\poly(p, k)$.
   717	  Then, the algorithm of Lenstra~\cite[Theorem 1.1]{lenstra1991finding} shows
   718	  that given such an irreducible polynomial, the multiplication table of a
   719	  normal basis of $\F_{p^k}$ over $\Fp$ can be computed in $\poly(k,\log p)$
   720	  time.
   721	  Finally, the algorithm of Wang~\cite{wang1989algorithm} shows that for odd $k$
   722	  and a multiplication table $K$ of a normal basis of $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$, a
   723	  multiplication table $K'$ for a self-dual normal basis of $\F_{2^k}$ over
   724	  $\F_2$ can be computed in $\poly(k)$ time.
   725	  Putting these three algorithms together yields the claimed statement.
   726	\end{proof}
   727	
   728	For $q=2^k$ for $k$ odd (i.e.\ $q$ is an admissible field size) we use the shorthand $\tr$ for $\tr_{q\to 2}$.
   729	
   730	\begin{lemma}
   731	  \label{lem:one}
   732	  Let $k$ be an odd integer and $\{e_i\}_{i=1}^k$ be a self-dual normal basis of
   733	  $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$.
   734	  Then $\tr(e_i) = 1$ for all $i$, and furthermore the representation
   735	  $\downsize(1)$ of the unit $1 \in \F_{2^k}$ is the all ones vector in
   736	  $\F_2^k$.
   737	\end{lemma}
   738	
   739	\begin{proof}
   740	  Since $\{e_i \}$ is a normal basis, $e_i = \alpha^{2^i}$ for some element
   741	  $\alpha \in \F_{2^k}$.
   742	  Furthermore, for every element $b \in \F_{2^k}$, we have that $\tr(b^2) =
   743	  \tr(b)$.
   744	  This is because
   745	  \[
   746	    \tr(b^2) = \sum_{i=0}^{k-1} b^{2^{i+1}} =
   747	    \sum_{i = 0}^{k-1} b^{2^i} = \tr(b)\;,
   748	  \]
   749	  where we use that $b^{2^k} = b$ for all $b \in \F_{2^k}$.
   750	  Since $e_{i+1} = e_i^2$, we get that $\tr(e_i) = \tr(e_j)$ for all $i,j$.
   751	  It cannot be the case that $\tr(e_i) = 0$ for all $i$.
   752	  Suppose that this were the case.
   753	  This would imply that $\tr(b) = 0$ for all $b \in \F_{2^k}$.
   754	  But then for all $j \in \{1, \ldots, k\}$ and for some $b \neq 0$, we would
   755	  also have by item 1 of \Cref{lem:downsize_field} that $b_j = \tr(b e_j) = 0$ where $b = \sum_j b_j e_j$ with $b_j \in
   756	  \F_2$.
   757	  This implies that $b$ is the all zero element of $\F_{2^k}$, which is a
   758	  contradiction.
   759	  Thus $\tr(e_i) = 1$ for all $i=1, 2, \ldots, k$.
   760	
   900	\label{lem:ld-encoding-complexity}
   901	Let $q$ be an admissible field size, and let $M = 2^m$ for some integer $m$.
   902	The complexity of computing the evaluation of the low-degree encoding $g_a(x)$,
   903	given $a \in \F_q^M$ and $x \in \F_q^m$ represented in binary, is $\poly(M,\log
   904	q)$.
   905	\end{lemma}
   906	\begin{proof}
   907		Computing $g_a(x)$ requires computing the sum of products $a_y \cdot
   908	  \ind_{m,y}(x)$ over all $y \in \{0,1\}^m$.
   909	  Via \Cref{lem:efficient_arithmetic}, evaluating $\ind_{m,y}(x)$ takes time
   910	  $\poly(m,\log q)$ because it requires performing $m$ multiplications of $\F_q$
   911	  elements, and therefore the product $a_y \cdot \ind_{m,y}(x)$ requires
   912	  $\poly(m,\log q)$ time.
   913	  Computing the sum over all $y \in \{0,1\}^m$ requires $M \cdot \poly(m,\log q)
   914	  = \poly(M,\log q)$ time, as claimed.
   915	\end{proof}

   926	\subsection{Linear spaces and registers}
   927	\label{sec:lin-reg}
   928	
   929	For a set $V$, we write $\C^V$ for the complex vector space of dimension $|V|$.
   930	The space $\C^V$ is endowed with a canonical orthonormal basis
   931	$\{\ket{x}\}_{x\in V}$.
   932	By ``a quantum state on $V$'' we mean a unit vector
   933	\begin{equation*}
   934	  \ket{\psi}_V \in \complex^V\;.
   935	\end{equation*}
   936	If $V = \bigoplus_{i=1}^k V_k$ is the direct sum of subspaces $V_k$ over $\F$,
   937	then $\complex^V$ can be identified with $\bigotimes_{i=1}^k
   938	\complex^{V_i}$, by the identification of $\ket{x_1 \oplus \dots \oplus
   939	  x_k}$ with $\ket{x_1} \otimes \dots \otimes \ket{x_k}$.
   940	As a special case, if $\{e_i\}$ is a basis of $V$ the decomposition $V =
   941	\bigoplus_{i=1}^k ( \F e_i)$ yields the tensor product decomposition $\C^V =
   942	\bigotimes_{i=1}^k \C^{\abs{\F}}$.
   943	We sometimes refer to the spaces $\C^{\abs{\F}}$ as the ``qudits'' of $\C^V$ (or
   944	of a state on it).
   945	
   946	\begin{definition}
   947	  \label{def:EPR}
   948	  For a linear space $V$ over a finite field $\F$, define the \EPR state on $\C^V
   949	  \otimes \C^V$ by
   950	  \begin{equation*}
   951	    \ket{\EPR}_V = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\abs{V}}} \sum_{x\in V}\ket {x}\otimes \ket{x}\;.
   952	  \end{equation*}
   953	  We also write $\ket{\EPR}_{\F_q}$ as $\ket{\EPR_q}$ and $\ket{\EPR_2}$ as
   954	  $\ket{\EPR}$.
   955	\end{definition}

   959	Quantum measurements are modeled as positive operator-valued
   960	measures (POVMs).
   961	A POVM consists of a set of positive semidefinite operators $\{ M_a \}_{a\in S}$
   962	indexed by outcomes $a\in S$ that satisfy the condition $\sum_a M_a = I$. If the latter condition is relaxed to $\sum_a M_a \leq I$ then we refer to $\{M_a\}$ as a \emph{sub-measurement}.

   964	defining the POVM.
   965	The probability that the measurement returns outcome $a$ on state $\ket{\psi}$
   966	is given by
   967	\begin{equation*}
   968	  \Pr(a) = \bra{\psi} M_a \ket{\psi}\;.
   969	\end{equation*}

  1052	\subsection{Generalized Pauli observables}
  1053	\label{sec:generalized-pauli}
  1054	
  1055	
  1056	For prime number $p$, the generalized Pauli operators over $\Fp$ are a
  1057	collection of observables indexed by a basis setting $X$ or $Z$ and an element
  1058	$a$ or $b$ of $\Fp$, with eigenvalues that are $p$-th roots of unity.
  1059	They are given by
  1060	\begin{equation}
  1061	  \label{eq:pauli-fp}
  1062	  \sigma^X(a) = \sum_{j \in \Fp} \ket{j + a} \bra{j}\qquad \text{and} \qquad
  1063	  \sigma^Z(b) = \sum_{j \in \Fp} \omega^{bj} \ket{j} \bra{j}\;,
  1064	\end{equation}
  1065	where $\omega = e^{\frac{2\pi i}{p}}$, and addition and multiplication are over
  1066	$\Fp$.
  1067	These observables obey the ``twisted commutation'' relations
  1068	\begin{equation}
  1069	  \label{eq:twisted-fp}
  1070	  \forall a,b\in\Fp\;,\qquad \sigma^X(a)\, \sigma^Z(b) =
  1071	  \omega^{-ab} \,\sigma^Z(b)\,\sigma^X(a)\;.
  1072	\end{equation}
  1073	Similarly, over a field $\Fq$ with $q$ a power of $p$, we can consider a set of generalized Pauli
  1074	operators, indexed by a basis setting $X$ or $Z$ and an element of $\Fq$ and
  1075	with eigenvalues that are $p$-th roots of unity.
  1076	For $a, b\in\Fq$ they are given by
  1077	\begin{equation*}
  1078	  \qp^X(a) = \sum_{j \in \Fq} \ket{j+a}\bra{j} \qquad \text{and} \qquad
  1079	  \qp^Z(b)= \sum_{j \in \Fq} \omega^{\tr(b j)} \ket{j}\bra{j}\;,
  1080	\end{equation*}
  1081	where addition and multiplication are over $\Fq$.
  1082	For all $W \in \{X,Z\}$, $a, a' \in \Fq$, and $b \in \Fp$, powers of these
  1083	observables obey the relations
  1084	\begin{equation*}\label{eq:pauli-product-power}
  1085	  \bigl(\qp^W(a)\qp^W(a')\bigr) = \qp^W(a+a') \qquad \text{and}
  1086	  \qquad \bigl( \qp^W(a) \bigr)^b = \qp^W(a b) \;.
  1087	\end{equation*}
  1088	In particular, since $pa=0$ for any $a\in \Fq$ we get that that $(\qp^W(a))^p =
  1089	I$ for any $a\in\Fq$.
  1090	The observables obey analogous ``twisted commutation'' relations
  1091	to~\eqref{eq:twisted-fp},
  1092	\begin{equation}
  1093	  \label{eq:twisted-fq}
  1094	  \forall a, b \in \Fq\;, \qquad \qp^X(a)\, \qp^Z(b) =
  1095	  \omega^{-\tr(a b)} \, \qp^Z(b)\, \qp^X(a)\;.
  1096	\end{equation}
  1097	It is clear from the definition that all of the $\qp^X$ operators commute with
  1098	each other, and similarly all the $\qp^Z$ operators commute with each other.
  1099	Thus, it is meaningful to speak of a common eigenbasis for all $\qp^X$
  1100	operators, and a common eigenbasis for all $\qp^Z$ operators.
  1101	The common eigenbasis for the $\qp^Z$ operators is the computational
  1102	basis $\{\ket{j}\}_{j \in \F_q}$.
  1103	To map this basis to the common eigenbasis of the $\qp^X$ operators, one can
  1104	apply the Fourier transform
  1105	\begin{equation}
  1106	  \label{eq:fourier-f}
  1107	  F \,=\, \frac{1}{\sqrt{q}} \sum_{a, b\in \Fq} \omega^{-\tr(ab)}
  1108	  \ket{a}\bra{b}\;.
  1109	\end{equation}
  1110	Explicitly, the eigenbases consist of the vectors $\ket{e_W}$ labeled by an
  1111	element $e \in \Fq$ and $W \in \{X, Z\}$, given by
  1112	\begin{equation*}
  1113	  \ket{e_X} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{q}} \sum_j \omega^{- \tr(e j)} \ket{j}\;, \qquad
  1114	  \ket{e_Z}   = \ket{e}\;.
  1115	\end{equation*}
  1116	We denote the POVM whose elements are projectors onto basis vectors of the
  1117	eigenbasis associated with the observables $\qp^W$ by $\{\qp^W_e\}_e$.
  1118	Then for all $W \in \{X,Z\}$ and $a\in \Fq$, the observables $\qp^W(a)$ can be
  1119	written as
  1120	\begin{equation}\label{eq:pauli-obs-proj-single}
  1121	  \qp^W(a) = \sum_{b \in \Fq} \omega^{\tr(a b)} \qp^W_b\;.
  1122	\end{equation}
  1123	
  1124	To invert this relation, we first quote the following useful Fourier fact.
  1125	\begin{lemma}[Fact 3.2 of \cite{NW19}]
  1126	  \label{lem:cancellation}

  1128	  \begin{equation*}

  1133	
  1134	We may now invert~\Cref{eq:pauli-obs-proj-single}:

  1143	Slightly abusing notation, for $W \in \{X, Z\}$ and $a \in \Fq^n$ we denote by

   215	\subsection{Distance measures}
   216	
   217	We introduce several distance measures that are used throughout.
   218	
   219	\begin{definition}[Distance between states]
   220	  \label{def:state-distance}
   221	
   222		Let $\{\ket{\psi_n}\}_{n\in \N}$ and $\{\ket{\psi'_n}\}_{n\in \N}$ be two
   223	  families of states in the same space $\mH$.
   224	  For some function $\delta : \N \to [0,1]$ we say that $\{ \ket{\psi_n} \}$ and
   225	  $\{ \ket{\psi'_n} \}$ are \emph{$\delta$-close}, denoted as $\ket{\psi}
   226	  \approx_\delta \ket{\psi'}$, if $ \norm{\ket{\psi_n} - \ket{\psi'_n}}^2 =
   227	  O(\delta(n))$.
   228	  (For convenience we generally leave the dependence of the states and $\delta$
   229	  on the indexing parameter $n$ implicit, writing e.g.\ $\ket{\psi}$ for $\ket{\psi_n}$.)
   230	\end{definition}
   231	
   232	\begin{definition}[Consistency between POVMs]
   233	  \label{def:consistency}
   234		Let $\mX$ be a finite set and $\mu$ a distribution on $\mX$.
   235	  Let $\ket{\psi} \in \cal{H}_A \otimes \cal{H}_B$ be a quantum state, and for
   236	  all $x\in \mX$, $\{A^x_a\}$ and $\{B^x_a\}$ POVMs.
   237	  We write
   238	  \begin{equation*}
   239	    A^x_a \otimes I_\bob \simeq_\delta I_\alice \otimes B^x_a
   240	  \end{equation*}
   241	  on state $\ket{\psi}$ and distribution $\mu$ if
   242	  \begin{equation*}
   243	    \E_{x\sim \mu} \sum_{a\ne b} \bra{\psi} A^x_a \otimes B^x_b \ket{\psi}
   244	    = O(\delta)\;.\footnote{Here the use of the $O(\cdot)$ notation refers to the fact that the notation will often be used to measure consistency for \emph{famillies} of POVM and states indexed by an implicit parameter $n\in \mathbb{N}$, which will always be clear from context but omitted for legibility, see Definition~\ref{def:state-distance}. The $O(\cdot)$ is taken as $n\to\infty$.}

    33	The game $\game^\ld$ is parametrized by a tuple $\ldparams = (q, m, d, \ldc)$
    34	where $m, d, \ldc \in \N$ are integers, $q \in \N$ is an admissible field size,
    35	and $m$ divides $q$.
    36	We sometimes write $\game^\ld_\ldparams$ to emphasize the dependence of the
    37	classical low-degree test on the parameter tuple $\ldparams$.
    38	
    39	We first provide a high-level description of the game for $k=1$.
    40	It is based on the low-individual degree variant of the multilinearity test
    41	of~\cite{babai1991non}, where one player (called the ``points player'') receives
    42	a random point $u \in \F_q^m$, and the other player (called the ``lines
    43	player'') receives a random axis-parallel line $\line$ that contains $u$, i.e.\
    44	the line parallel to the $i$-th axis which goes through point $u$, for uniformly
    45	random $i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}$.
    46	The points player is supposed to respond with a value $a \in \F_q$, and the
    47	lines player is supposed to respond with a univariate polynomial $f_\line$ of
    48	degree at most $d$ such that $f_\line(u_i) = a$, where $u_i$ is the $i$-th
    49	coordinate of $u$.
    50	
    51	Suppose the players agree beforehand on a global polynomial $g: \F_q^m \to \F_q$
    52	such that every variable has degree at most $d$.
    53	Then a winning strategy is the following: the points player responds with
    54	$g(u)$, and the lines player responds with the univariate polynomial $f_\line$
    55	that is the restriction of $g$ to line $\line$; formally, for $t \in \F_q$,
    56	\[f_\line(t)=g(u_1,u_2,\ldots,u_{i-1},t,u_{i+1},\ldots,u_m)\;.\] It is easy to
    57	see that $f_\line(t)$ has degree at most $d$ in the variable $t$.
    58	Thus in this case the players will pass the low-degree test with probability
    59	$1$.
    60	The low-degree testing theorem states that the converse approximately holds: if
    61	the players pass the low-degree test with probability close to $1$, then their
    62	responses must be approximately consistent (in some sense) with a global
    63	polynomial $g$ with individual degree $d$.
    64	
    65	When $k > 1$, the players are supposed to respond with a \emph{tuple} of
    66	answers; and the test is intended to check that the players' responses are
    67	consistent with a $k$-tuple of functions $g_i: \F_q^m \to \F_q$ that are
    68	polynomials where every variable has degree at most $d$.

   902	We start by discussing parameter settings.
   903	The game $\game^\pauli$ is parametrized by a tuple
   904	\[\qldparams = (q,m,d)\;,\] where $q,m,d \in \N$ are integers. 
   905	We sometimes write $\game^\pauli_\qldparams$ to emphasize the dependence of the
   906	Pauli basis test on the parameters.
   907	
   908	Informally, the test is meant to certify that the players share a state of the
   909	form $\ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes M}$, where $M=2^m$.
   910	Its question set includes questions that are axis-parallel/diagonal lines and points in $\F_q^m$,
   911	which are meant to correspond to questions in the classical low-degree test, and questions
   912	of the form $(\Pauli, W)$, for $W \in \{X, Z\}$.
   913	Upon receipt of a question of the latter form, the players are expected to
   914	perform the POVM $\{\tau_h^W\}_{h \in \F_q^{M}}$ and report the outcome $h$ as
   915	their answer.
   916	
   917	The key idea behind the test
   918	is for the provers to encode their outcomes using the \emph{low-degree encoding} from Section~\ref{sec:ld-encoding}.
   919	Given an outcome $h \in \F_q^M$, the low-degree encoding of~$h$ is the polynomial $g_h:\F_q^m \rightarrow \F_q$.
   920	Rather than asking the provers to always return the entire string~$h$,
   921	many of the subtests in the game $\game^\pauli$ will ``probe'' limited information about~$h$ as follows:
   922	the verifier provides the provers with a string $u_W \in \F_q^m$,
   923	and using this they are expected to evaluate $g_h(u_W) \in \F_q$ and return it to the verifier.
   924	For a fixed value of~$W$, then, the prover's responses to these ``probes'' should be consistent with some low-degree polynomial in the input~$u_W$.
   925	To check this, the verifier can perform the classical low-degree test from Section~\ref{sec:ld-verifier}.
   926	This ensures that the prover's responses for the $W = X$ basis are consistent with each other,
   927	as well as their responses for the $W = Z$ basis, although it does not test consistency between the $X$ and $Z$ responses.
   928	
   929	The next set of subtests the verifier performs ensure that the provers' $X$ and $Z$ measurements are consistent with each other.
   930	On the $X$ side, consider the measurement in which the prover performs the $\{\tau_h^X\}$ POVM,
   931	receives outcome $h_X$, and outputs $g_{h_X}(u_X) \in \F_q$.
   932	For technical reasons that will become clear shortly,
   933	it will be convenient for the prover's measurement to have two outcomes rather than~$q$ outcomes.
   934	To accomplish this, the verifier also provides the prover with an element $r_X \in \F_q$;
   935	given this, the prover should output not $g_{h_X}(u_X) \in \F_q$ but $\tr(g_{h_X}(u_X) \cdot r_X)$, which is an element of $\F_2$.
   936	Similarly, on the $Z$ side, suppose the prover is provided $r_Z \in \F_q$,
   937	performs $\{\tau_h^Z\}$ to receive $h_Z$, and outputs $\tr(g_{h_Z}(u_Z) \cdot r_Z) \in \F_2$.
   938	Together, these two are a pair of two-outcome measurements, one in the~$X$ basis and one in the~$Z$ basis,
   939	and as it turns out, this pair of measurements either commutes with each other or anticommutes with each other
   940	(this is why we modified the measurements to have only two outcomes).
   941	The key quantity to determine which of these is the case is the following complicated-looking expression:
   942	\begin{equation*}
   943	\gamma = \tr \bigl( (\ind_{m}(u_\xpt) \cdot r_\xpt) \cdot
   944	      (\ind_{m}(u_\zpt) \cdot r_\zpt) \bigr)\;.
   945	\end{equation*}
   946	If $\gamma = 0$, then these two measurements commute, and if $\gamma = 1$, then these two measurements anticommute
   947	(this fact is established in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:pauli-completeness} below).
   948	In the $\gamma = 0$ case, the verifier can check whether these two measurements commute by performing the ``commutation check'',
   949	which asks the provers to simultaneously measure both $\tr(g_{h_X}(u_X) \cdot r_X)$ and $\tr(g_{h_Z}(u_Z) \cdot r_Z)$ and report their values.
   950	In the $\gamma = 1$ case, on the other hand, the measurements anticommute, which implies that they cannot simultaneously be measured.
   951	In spite of this, the verifier can still check that the measurements anticommute by using the Magic Square game from Section~\ref{sec:ms} above.
   952	As was shown in Theorem~\ref{thm:ms-from-ac}, any pair of anticommuting measurements
   953	can be used to form a perfect strategy for the Magic Square game
   954	(and indeed the reverse is true as well: any perfect strategy for the Magic Square game entails a pair of anticommuting measurements).
   955	
   956	Together, these give the main subtests for the game $\game^\pauli$.

def binaryRepresentation {q : ℕ} (F : FixedFieldModel q) : F.K ≃ Fin q :=
  binaryEquiv F

/--

`def:subfields-kappa` in `blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:182-208`,
whose paper origin is `references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:89-93`.

noncomputable abbrev kappa {F K ι : Type*} [CommSemiring F] [Semiring K]
    [Algebra F K] [Finite ι]
    (b : Module.Basis ι F K) : K ≃ₗ[F] (ι → F) :=
  b.equivFun

`Algebra.leftMulMatrix`.  It is the multiplication table `K_a` in
`def:subfields-kappa` (blueprint lines 196-199; paper
`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:89-93`).

noncomputable abbrev multiplicationTable {F K ι : Type*} [CommSemiring F]
    [Semiring K] [Algebra F K] [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
    (b : Module.Basis ι F K) : K →ₐ[F] Matrix ι ι F :=
  Algebra.leftMulMatrix b

noncomputable abbrev binTrace (K : Type*) [CommRing K] [Algebra (ZMod 2) K] :
    K →ₗ[ZMod 2] ZMod 2 :=
  Algebra.trace (ZMod 2) K
